 What the wattage labels really mean 
 Total output is a shared budget
 A charger’s total-wattage figure describes the maximum power available across its ports, not a promise that every connected device receives that amount. When several devices are attached, the charger’s internal power-allocation rules divide the available budget. A laptop that negotiates a high-power profile can therefore receive less when a phone, tablet or accessory is plugged in.
 UGREEN’s cited four-port listing specifies its overall rating and identifies two ports capable of the highest listed individual output. That makes the first two USB-C positions the ones to reserve for a demanding laptop or other high-draw device. The listing does not establish that all four ports can simultaneously operate at their individual maxima.
 Anker’s A2687 likewise has a total ceiling that is different from its highest single-port figure. The 150W number is a supported mode for one port, not the charger’s total rating and not the official product name. Treat it as a negotiated profile available when the connected device, cable and charger state all support it.
 Why a laptop may not draw the headline figure
 USB-C Power Delivery is negotiated between the charger and the device. The laptop requests a profile it understands, then limits intake based on its own firmware, battery state, temperature, workload and charging design. A machine advertised with a high-wattage USB-C input may still choose a lower profile with either charger. The cable also has to be rated for the requested current and power.
 For that reason, a higher single-port number is not proof of shorter charging time. It can matter when your particular laptop accepts that profile, but it does not override the laptop’s input limit or the power distribution that occurs after other devices are connected.

 Port count and simultaneous charging 
 When the four-port UGREEN layout is the better fit
 If you routinely charge a laptop, phone, tablet, watch, earbuds or another USB device at the same time, a fourth connection can eliminate a separate low-power adapter. The UGREEN listing is explicitly for a four-port model, so it is the logical choice when connection count is your first constraint. Confirm the connector types and regional configuration before ordering; the four-port listing should not be inferred from reviews of another Nexode Pro design.
 When Anker’s three USB-C ports are enough
 The A2687 is a three-port USB-C charger. That is a clean arrangement for a laptop, phone and tablet when all three devices use USB-C, and it avoids needing a USB-A cable. It is less convenient if you need four devices attached or if one of your everyday accessories still requires a different connector.
 Port count alone does not tell you the power each port will receive during simultaneous use. Before choosing, write down the devices you normally connect together and check the manufacturer’s output-distribution chart for the exact regional model. A charger that has the right number of sockets but reallocates power away from your laptop may be less useful than one with fewer ports and a distribution pattern that matches your routine.
 A practical simultaneous-use worksheet
 List the devices you charge together. Record the laptop’s required USB-C input, the phone or tablet’s preferred fast-charge standard, and any low-power accessories.
 Mark the device that must maintain performance while plugged in. This is usually the laptop, a gaming handheld or another device being used under load.
 Reserve the charger’s highest-capability port for that device. On the UGREEN listing, that means one of the two ports identified for the highest individual output.
 Check the multi-port allocation table for the exact SKU. Do not assume the single-port figure remains available after adding two or three devices.
 Choose the model whose remaining ports match your cables. A nominally powerful port is not useful if your daily accessories cannot connect without extra adapters.
 Charging protocols and cable requirements 
 UGREEN’s published protocol coverage
 UGREEN’s Nexode Pro family page says the family supports PD, QC, SCP, AFC and PPS, and describes compatibility with modern smartphones, tablets and laptops. It also mentions 45W Samsung Super Fast Charging 2.0. Those are family-level statements; they do not prove that every Nexode Pro variant exposes every protocol at every port or that every device reaches its maximum rate.
 For a purchase decision, match the protocol your device actually uses rather than counting protocol names. A laptop normally depends on USB Power Delivery, while some phones select a manufacturer-specific or PPS profile. If your phone’s fastest mode requires a particular protocol, verify that the exact four-port listing supports it on the port you plan to use.

The device and cable still have to request and carry a matching profile.
 The Prime Power Bank condition
 Anker describes up to 150W recharging for a compatible Anker Prime Power Bank when AI Mode 2.0 is active and the specified cable is used. The charger does not include that cable, according to Anker. This is a particular accessory-and-mode combination, not a general promise that any power bank will accept 150W from the A2687.
 If this use case is your reason for buying the Anker charger, verify four things before checkout: that your power-bank model is one of the compatible Prime versions, that AI Mode 2.0 is available on your device and current firmware, that the cable meets Anker’s stated requirements, and that the feature is offered in your country. A generic USB-C cable can work for ordinary charging yet fail to expose this special profile.

 What is established for the A2687
 The A2687 is sold as a Smart Display model. Anker also presents app or mode-related controls as part of the product experience. These features can help you inspect charging status or select a supported operating mode, but they do not change the charger’s total electrical limit. If you prefer a screen and Anker’s software-oriented controls, they are legitimate reasons to favor this model even when your raw wattage needs would be met by either charger.

Its built-in 70 cm cable and foldable pins may reduce packing clutter, but those features do not describe the four-port charger compared in the main table. Verify the variant before treating the review as purchase evidence.
 A decision process that avoids the wattage trap 
 Identify the exact SKU. Select the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 4-Port listing or the Anker A2687 listing, not a search result that combines several similarly named products.
 Count simultaneous connections. Pick four-port UGREEN if you genuinely need four connections and its confirmed connector layout fits; pick three-port Anker if three USB-C devices cover your routine.
 Check the demanding device’s input requirement. Compare your laptop or other high-draw device’s accepted USB-C Power Delivery profiles with the charger’s published port capability.
 Verify cable ratings. Use a cable rated for the requested power. For the Prime Power Bank’s special recharge mode, use the cable specified by Anker; it is not supplied with the charger.
 Review multi-port power allocation. Look at the exact regional listing and decide whether your laptop will retain enough power when the other devices are connected.
 Check regional details. Confirm plug format, electrical input range, connector configuration, stock and firmware-dependent features for your country.
 Choose features only after compatibility. A smart display, app controls or a retractable cable can improve convenience, but they cannot compensate for missing ports or an unsupported charging protocol.
 What the available evidence can—and cannot—tell you 
 The manufacturer pages establish the published output, ports, protocols and dimensions listed above. They do not establish which charger runs cooler, sustains its maximum output longer, charges a particular laptop faster, or has a lower long-term failure rate.
 No controlled head-to-head test was available for these exact products. The hands-on article covers the retractable-cable UGREEN variant rather than the four-port model, and it is not a comparison with Anker. Therefore, claims about a measured temperature winner, efficiency winner or universal charging-time winner would go beyond the evidence.
 Prices and promotions are also volatile. A current sale price, stock status or regional bundle should be checked at the time you buy rather than inferred from an older listing. The same caution applies to firmware-dependent modes and country-specific plug versions.
 Buying checklist 
 Confirm the full product name and model number, especially for the UGREEN charger.
 Verify the number and type of ports on the exact regional listing.
 Compare your laptop’s required USB-C Power Delivery profile with the charger’s port specification.
 Check the charger’s power-allocation table for the number of devices you normally connect.
 Use appropriately rated USB-C cables; do not assume every cable supports the highest advertised mode.
 If buying the Anker for Prime Power Bank charging, confirm AI Mode 2.0, compatible hardware and the required cable.
 Confirm plug format, input voltage, dimensions, weight and availability for your country.
 Keep the purchase receipt and model information so support can distinguish the four-port UGREEN unit from the retractable-cable version.
 Bottom-line recommendation 
 Buy the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 4-Port when four connections are the deciding requirement and the exact listing’s port layout and power distribution match your devices. Buy the Anker Prime A2687 when three USB-C ports, its Smart Display and related controls, or the conditional Prime Power Bank recharge mode are more valuable than a fourth connection.

 List every device you will charge at once. Include laptops, phones, tablets, watches, earbuds, cameras and power banks. Note which use USB-C and which still require USB-A.

 Decide whether you need three or four connections. Count the ports you need simultaneously rather than counting devices you own.
 Account for shared power. If you need a high-power laptop charge while also charging a tablet and phone, inspect the manufacturer’s multi-port output table and expect the available wattage to be divided.

 A laptop is charging below its expected wattage
 Confirm that the laptop’s USB-C port accepts charging at the requested level; some USB-C ports support data or display only.
 Use a cable rated for the laptop’s required wattage.
 Disconnect other devices temporarily. Shared output can reduce the laptop’s allocation.
 Try the charger’s highest-output USB-C port: USB-C1 or USB-C2 on the cited UGREEN listing, or the port specified for the desired mode on A2687.
 Check the laptop’s charging indicator after reconnecting. A lower negotiated rate can reflect the laptop’s own thermal or battery-management limit rather than a charger fault.
 The phone does not show its fastest charging mode
 Verify that the phone supports the protocol involved, such as PPS, QC, AFC or a manufacturer-specific mode.
 Use a compatible cable and remove hubs or adapters that can alter negotiation.
 Test with only the phone connected so the charger is not reallocating power.
 Remember that family-level protocol support does not guarantee maximum speed on every handset.
 The Prime Power Bank does not recharge at 150W
 Confirm that the power bank is a compatible Prime model.
 Enable or select AI Mode 2.0 if the power bank requires it.
 Use the cable supplied for the feature or a replacement explicitly compatible with the required Anker Protocol profile.
 Connect the power bank directly to A2687 and remove other loads while testing.
 Allow the power bank and charger to reach normal operating conditions; the 150W statement is a conditional maximum, not a guaranteed constant rate.

 Disconnect all devices, reconnect the highest-priority device first, then add the others one at a time. This reveals whether a particular cable, accessory or combination is causing renegotiation. If the behavior persists with different cables and a single device, stop using that setup and contact the manufacturer rather than continuing to cycle a potentially faulty charger.

 Current sale prices and promotions are volatile, and the available specifications do not provide a comparable price check. Compare the exact SKU, included cable, plug type, warranty terms and return policy in your country instead of relying on a “160W” label shared by multiple variants.
 For UGREEN, make sure the listing is explicitly the 4-port charger if you need that layout. For Anker, look for model A2687 and the official 160W product name.  Verdict
 Buy the UGREEN Nexode Pro 160W 4-Port when your deciding factor is an additional port or the ability to draw up to 140W from either of its two specified high-output USB-C ports. Buy the Anker Prime Charger (160W, 3 Ports, Smart Display), A2687 when three USB-C ports meet your needs, its display and associated features matter, or you specifically use the compatible Prime Power Bank’s conditional 150W AI Mode 2.0 recharge.
 Both are 160W-class chargers, so headline wattage alone should not decide the purchase. Match the exact variant to your connectors, cables, devices and simultaneous charging plan; that is the distinction the product names conceal.

 FAQ 
 1. 
 What is Power Delivery?
 USB-C and USB PD are often confused, but the important thing to remember is that USB-C is a reversible connection type, while USB PD is a power delivery specification, overseen by the USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF) and often expressed simply as ‘PD’. With version 3.1 of the specification, Power Delivery is able to carry up to 240W of power plus data over USB-C (previously limited to 100W on PD 3.0), but devices that support Power Delivery can range from 18W right up to 240W.
 2. 
 How much power do I need to charge my laptop?
 The easiest way to find out how much power is required to charge your laptop is to inspect the charger that was sold with it, if you have that to hand. Alternatively you can look for its specification on the manufacturer’s website. 
 You’re looking for a figure in watts, although it may be expressed in volts and amps. If so, simply multiply these two numbers to get the figure you need. For example, a device that requires 12V/2A to charge will need a 24W USB-C PD charger (12 x 2 = 24).
 Once you know what power rating you’re looking for, finding a USB-C PD charger for your laptop or console is easy. Sometimes it can pay to get one a little faster than you need—it may be more expensive, but you’ll be pleased you bought it if you later decide to upgrade your laptop.
 3. 
 Can I use a more powerful third-party charger than the one supplied with my laptop?
 Yes. There is no need to worry about plugging devices into chargers that are capable of delivering more power than the device is able to accept, since USB devices will draw only the power they need. However, the cable you use to join the two is crucial, and using a low-quality or under-specified cable with the charger could lead to problems with your device. Read more about the differences in USB-C cables before you buy .
 4. 
 Why won’t my laptop charge from a third-party charger?
 Although USB PD can go as high as 240W, actual speeds supported by chargers can vary—it’s possible that your third-party adaptor is not powerful enough to charge your laptop.
 The adaptor itself is only one piece of the puzzle, and the cable with which it is combined must also be capable of delivering the required amount of power. Read more about the differences in USB-C cables before you buy .
 5. 
 What is the advantage of a GaN charger?
 GaN is short for gallium nitride. It requires fewer components than traditional silicone chargers, which means devices that use the technology can be less bulky and more efficient.
 6. 
 Can all PD laptop chargers fast-charge smartphones?
 If you’re looking to fast-charge a smartphone that promises charging of, say, 65W, do note that many third-party USB PD chargers will not support protocols such as PPS (Programmable Power Supply) or SCP (Super Charge Protocol) that is required by proprietary phone fast-charging standards. You can expect 18W charging from such devices, regardless of the theoretical output of the USB-C port.

The 160W figure is a ceiling for the charger as a whole, not 140W or 160W simultaneously from every connector. When several devices are plugged in, the charger must divide its available output according to its power-allocation rules and each device’s request.
 For example, a laptop connected to USB-C1 may be eligible for the advertised 140W only while the other ports are idle or within the allocation permitted by UGREEN’s table. Adding a phone, tablet or accessory can reduce the power offered to the laptop. That is normal behavior for a multi-port charger and not evidence of a defect.

 A2687’s total rating is also 160W. Anker lists up to 150W from one port in a supported operating mode. That number does not make the product a 150W-total charger, and it does not imply that all three ports can deliver their maximum ratings at once. A laptop must also support the relevant USB Power Delivery profile and be connected with a suitable cable.
 Anker separately says that up to 150W recharging is available for its compatible Prime Power Bank in AI Mode 2.0. The charger’s single-port specification and the power bank’s special recharge feature are related but not interchangeable claims. Neither means that an arbitrary USB-C laptop, phone or battery will accept 150W.
 Why a higher headline number may not charge your device faster
 Actual charging rate is limited by the device, its battery-management system, the negotiated protocol and the cable. A computer that accepts 100W cannot draw 140W or 150W merely because the wall charger advertises it. Connecting a second or third device can also change the power available to the first one. Treat the headline wattage as the charger’s capability, then check the device’s input specification and the output table for the exact port combination you plan to use.
 Charging is also dynamic. A laptop may request high power while its battery is low and taper the request as it fills. Phones can reduce intake when warm, and power banks may expose their highest mode only when a particular operating mode is enabled. A wattage display, where provided, should therefore be read as a momentary negotiated value rather than a guaranteed constant.

 The official A2687 product is rated at 160W total. Anker lists up to 150W as a supported single-port mode and separately describes up to 150W Prime Power Bank recharging under AI Mode 2.0 and compatible-cable conditions.

 Some laptops still ship with their own cumbersome AC power brick and barrel-shaped DC connector, but most premium laptops today also or solely charge via USB-C—including all the models in our roundup of the best laptops .
 Foundry
 USB-C chargers are much smaller and more convenient than proprietary chargers, and will work with multiple and varied devices, making them a more flexible, more portable solution.
 Thunderbolt ports on laptops are compatible with—and look identical to—USB-C, the reversible connector that is fast replacing the rectangular USB-A standard. 
 Of course, not every laptop with a USB-C port can be charged with a USB-C charger. The determining factor is support for USB Power Delivery ( PD ); more details below.
 Assuming that your laptop supports charging via USB-C, the following products reviewed are, in our estimation, the best USB-C PD chargers you can pair with your device. 
 For USB-C chargers you don’t need to buy an HP laptop charger to charge an HP laptop. Each of the third-party USB-C chargers tested and reviewed below will work with any laptop that supports USB PD charging. Note that cheaper low-quality chargers can pose a significant risk due to their lack of safety measures, and can lead to electric shocks or short circuits that could damage your laptop’s battery or cause a fire. Here, we have reviewed and highlighted only superior laptop chargers, ensuring top-end performance, safety, and compatibility.
 Which wattage charger do you need?
 Smaller laptops often require just a 35W or 45W charger, mid-sized need 65W, and larger laptops demand 100W or higher. 
 PD chargers will be rated at either PD 3.0 or PD 3.1. PD 3.0 can charge at up to 100W depending on the maximum output of the charging port; PD 3.1 at up to 240W, although few current laptops require anything over 140W. 
 Consider the total output of the charger when it has multiple ports. Most multi-port chargers are quite flexible in spreading that total output between ports. We have listed the default port maximums and the total all-port output for each charger reviewed.
 Also look for chargers offering Programmable Power Supply ( PPS ), which makes charging supported devices more efficient; note that not all devices support PPS. See below our list of the best chargers for more information on PD, PPS and other technologies.
 Different types of laptop charger

We have also chosen our best laptop charger for car , and even some fun laptop chargers that might even make you smile.

 What to look for in a USB-C PD charger
 As mentioned above, the primary requirement is that your laptop includes a USB-C port that can carry power as well as data. Older laptops that came with their own power brick might have data-only USB-C but not power-supporting USB-C.
 USB-C laptop chargers use a certified technology called USB Power Delivery (USB PD) , a specification that enables power delivery along with data over a single cable.
 All the chargers tested here are certified by the USB Implementers Forum (USB-IF), and are from reliable, trusted brands—you’ll find cheaper, less-well-known brands online but for safety’s sake we recommend you chose a proven brand, such as Anker, Ugreen, Satechi, Belkin, Plugable or Aukey, as well as big brands such as HP, Dell, Google and Samsung that follow the latest safety standards.
 Chargers can get hot, so you want to trust that yours won’t catch fire or otherwise damage your laptop. That’s why we avoid cheaper brands that we haven’t heard of or tested.
 USB PD 3.0 supports up to 100W of power to the laptop. USB PD 3.1 can reach 240W, which is useful for larger laptops that require over 100W for charging at full speed while in use, and for fast-charging compatible laptops.
 PPS support offers more efficient charging
 Some chargers support the USB-PD Programmable Power Supply (PPS) standard.
 PPS allows for a finer grain control of voltage. As my colleague Gordon Ung explains , while a standard USB-C charge rate can look like large steps, PPS can look like a curve and is constantly renegotiated every few seconds based on what the device’s battery tells the charger it needs. This can result in cooler charging inside the device as the conversion is offloaded to the charger rather than the device itself. In turn, this can lead to faster charging as well as less stress on the battery during charging, which can result in a longer service life for a battery.
 PPS requires the charged device to support the standard. While many Android phones and tablets support PPS, Apple devices do not. Non-supported devices will still work with the PPS charger as PPS chargers also support the universal USB PD standard; they just won’t charge as efficiently as PPS devices do.
 Wattage
 Once you know that your laptop supports USB PD charging, the most important specification to look for when choosing a laptop charger is the amount of power it can supply to your laptop—measured in watts (W).
 The wattage you should look for will depend on the maximum power draw of your laptop—that is, the draw when you are using a bunch of apps at the same time or pushing the graphics functions, not when you’re just browsing the web or sending emails. This level of maximum power is what the manufacturer considers when it decides on the wattage of the charger it includes with the laptop.
 When idle or doing mundane jobs that draw only a small amount of power from the charger, laptops can recharge fully on a lower-wattage charger—so a 45W charger can top up an idle 65W laptop but much slower than a 65W charger.
 That said, when buying a new USB-C charger, buy at least the same wattage as the charger that shipped with your laptop.
 Smaller laptops may require just a 30W or 45W charger, while medium laptops usually need 65W, and 100W is required for larger 15-inch and larger notebooks.
 Don’t worry if your laptop requires just 45W and you fancy that 100W charger—using a higher-power charger won’t harm your lower-powered laptop as it will regulate the power from the charger.
 Using a higher-wattage charger than your laptop requires is recommended when choosing a charger with multiple ports, as the stated wattage is the maximum output, and charging other devices at the same time will start lowering the power going to the laptop.
 For more charging questions answered, see our laptop charging FAQ at the end of this article.
 A charger with multiple ports can charge several gadgets at the same time, although remember that your laptop will be the hungriest for power and the charger will have a maximum output Ugreen
 Multiple ports for more devices
 Standard laptop chargers have just one USB-C port or connector, but many third-party USB-C chargers boast multiple ports—sometimes both USB-C and older USB-A.
 These are useful if you want to charge more than just your laptop—with multiple ports on your charger, you can power up your phone, tablet, or headphones at the same time as your laptop.
 If you want to use more than one charging port, consider your maximum requirement—say, 65W for the laptop and another 15W for a phone and maybe 5W for a smartwatch or headphones. A charger with a higher wattage can distribute the excess power to other connected devices at the same time as you power your laptop.
 Multi-port chargers will have a variety of charging options between ports and devices.
 Go for GaN
 Look for chargers built with modern Gallium Nitride (GaN) technology that runs cooler than older silicon tech, meaning that devices built with it can charge devices faster and with less heat dissipation than traditional chargers and are noticeably smaller, too.
 Newer GaN 2 can operate at even higher voltages and temperatures.
 Dimensions given in our reviews are for the U.S. models, which are also pictured for each product, but UK models are mostly also available. Due to their sturdy three-pin Type G plug, UK models are usually wider than their U.S. Type A and B plug counterparts.
 Fast charging 
 Modern laptops support fast charging, where the battery can be pumped up to at least 50 percent capacity—sometimes greater—in around 30 minutes.
 A laptop with fast-charging support is easier to keep close to a full charge. If the battery is fully drained, fast charging helps you get back to work fast, and you can quickly top up the battery when required—even just a few minutes of charging can save you when you don’t have much time near a power socket.
 Anker
 Choose the right charging cable
 Some USB-C laptop chargers ship with a cable, but most don’t. Make sure the cable you use supports power delivery, as some are for data-transfer only.
 The wisest choices for USB PD cables are based on the latest Thunderbolt 4 or USB4 standards, which are both backwards compatible with Thunderbolt 3 and USB-C, and supports both charging and up to 40Gbps data transfer. But Thunderbolt/USB4 is more expensive and often available in shorter lengths than USB-C cables.
 Look for a USB-C PD or Thunderbolt cable. If you want to charge at over 100W, this should support USB PD 3.1. Not all cables are marked as supporting 240W so make sure you check the PD rating before your purchase.
 Plugable sells 240W-supporting PD 3.1 charging cables that it labels Extended Power Range (EPR) in USB4 EPR or Thunderbolt 4 EPR —both are backwards compatible with USB-C. Anker’s 765 USB-C to USB-C Cable also supports PD 3.1.
 The maximum length for power cables is 2m. Anything longer, and less power will reach the connected device.
 Find more of the best USB-C cables in our roundup.
 Ugreen
 Wall charger or desktop charger
 A wall charger features plug prongs and connects directly into the wall power socket. Straight-to-socket wall chargers are small and portable—most will fit in your pocket. They might not have as many ports as a desktop charger but can still have several ports to choose from.
 If you carry your charger around with you a lot, look for a wall charger that has foldable plug prongs, which makes it more comfortable and smaller. These are more common with U.S. Type A plugs than UK Type G plugs.
 A desktop charger is separated from the socket by a power cable (usually detachable), with the charger instead sitting on your desk. Desktop chargers always feature multiple ports, and sometimes a separate power supply that will hide under the desk.
 They are great for keeping your device-charging organized and in one neat package but are usually less portable than wall chargers.
 There are also handy power strips with USB PD ports as well as extra sockets—useful in a home or office environment with few power sockets.
 Another laptop-charging solution is to use a docking station or hub . These boast even more ports than a desktop charger, such as HDMI/DisplayPort, ethernet, and card readers. Check out our recommended best Thunderbolt and USB-C DisplayLink docks and best USB-C hubs .
 FAQ 
 1. 
 Can I charge my laptop with USB-C?
 Probably. If your laptop supports USB PD (Power Delivery), you can charge it using a USB-C PD charger.
 It has to be USB PD for charging, as some USB-C ports are data only.
 If your laptop came with a USB-C port on its power adapter, then the answer is almost certainly yes, but you might want to check the product documentation or ask the manufacturer for clarification.
 2. 
 Can I charge my laptop with any USB-C charger?
 Probably. A few years back, some laptop manufacturers, such as HP, were fussy about which USB PD chargers would work with its products. But today, compatibility is mainly universal.
 3. 
 Can I use a charger with a higher wattage than my laptop?
 Yes. Power regulation means that it is safe to charge a 45W laptop with a 100W charger, for example. Laptops are designed to draw up to only a certain level of power when running at full speed.
 4. 
 Can a higher-wattage charger power-up a laptop faster?
 Possibly. A more powerful charger—with a higher wattage than the charger that shipped with your laptop—might charge your laptop a little faster, but this is certainly not guaranteed.
 5. 
 Can I use a charger with a lower wattage than my laptop?
 Yes, but you should try not to. You can charge a 100W laptop with a 65W charger, for example, but it’s not advisable as the laptop battery could drain faster than it is being charged, especially if in use at the time.
 Charging an idle laptop should mean that its battery will be fully charged with a lower-wattage charger, but it will take much longer than with the correctly rated charger. As a one-off it should be fine, but we do not recommend it in the long term. Using a lower-rated charger could result in overheating, which is never a good thing with electronics.
 6. 
 Will my laptop charge faster if not in use?
 Yes. When your laptop is idle or you are using only light apps such as email, it will be draining only a small amount of power from its battery, so it will charge faster. If you are using performance-hungry apps at the same time as charging, the charger will take longer to catch up as the laptop’s battery is constantly draining while in use.  
 7. 
 Can I charge my phone using a laptop charger?
 Yes, you can use a laptop charger to charge your phone. Some chargers feature more than one port, and the lower wattage ports are perfect for phone charging—but you can also charge a phone with a 140W charging port if you want to, although it’s safer for the phone if you use a lower-wattage port.
 8. 
 Can I use any cable to charge a laptop?
 No. You must use a USB-C cable that supports power delivery. Some USB-C cables can’t carry as much power as others. A USB PD 3.0 cable can carry 100W of power. A USB PD 3.1 cable can carry 240W of power.
 9. 
 Can I use a UBC-C cable to charge a Thunderbolt or USB4 laptop?
 Yes. Thunderbolt 3, Thunderbolt 4, and USB4 are backwards compatible with USB-C for data and charging.
 Thunderbolt and USB4 also have higher data-transfer bandwidth—up to 40Gbps—than USB-C, which is rated between 5Gbps and 20Gbps.
 10. 
 Can I use a Thunderbolt cable with a USB-C charger?
 Yes. Thunderbolt is backwards compatible with USB-C so a Thunderbolt cable can be used with a USB-C laptop or USB-C charger.
 You still need to ensure that the Thunderbolt cable can handle the right amount of power you require. All Thunderbolt 3 or 4 and USB4 cables can handle 100W of power, but some support up to 240W.
 11. 
 Should I charge my laptop to 100%?
 Only if you need to. If you are going on a road trip and need all the juice your laptop battery can supply, then by all means charge it to 100 percent before heading out.
 But it’s easier on the battery if you keep it charged between 40 and 80 percent—no lower and no higher if you can.
 Batteries charged to the full 100 percent might have only 300-500 discharge cycles, but batteries charged only up to 80 percent could get to nearly 4x that number of recharging cycles.
 12. 
 Should I fully drain my laptop battery to 0%?
 No. As with our advice not to fully charge a lithium-ion laptop battery too often, it’s better for long-term battery life if you keep it charged between 40 and 80 percent.
